3.1 Contrastive Learning as Dictionary Look-up
Contrastive learning [27], and its recent developments, can be thought of as training an encoder for a dictionary look-up task, as described next.

Consider an encoded query [MATH q] and a set of encoded samples [MATH \{k_{0},k_{1},k_{2},...\}] that are the keys of a dictionary. Assume that there is a single key (denoted as [MATH k_{+}] ) in the dictionary that [MATH q] matches. A contrastive loss [27] is a function whose value is low when [MATH q] is similar to its positive key [MATH k_{+}] and dissimilar to all other keys (considered negative keys for [MATH q] ). With similarity measured by dot product, a form of a contrastive loss function, called InfoNCE [44], is considered in this paper:
[MATH \small\mathcal{L}_{q}=-\log\frac{\exp(q{\cdot}k_{+}/\tau)}{\sum_{i=0}^{K}\exp(q{\cdot}k_{i}/\tau)}] (1)

where [MATH \tau] is a temperature hyper-parameter per [59]. The sum is over one positive and [MATH K] negative samples. Intuitively, this loss is the log loss of a [MATH ({K}{+}1)] -way softmax-based classifier that tries to classify [MATH q] as [MATH k_{+}] . Contrastive loss functions can also be based on other forms [27, 57, 59, 34], such as margin-based losses and variants of NCE losses.

The contrastive loss serves as an unsupervised objective function for training the encoder networks that represent the queries and keys [27]. In general, the query representation is [MATH q=f_{\textrm{q}}(x^{q})] where [MATH f_{\textrm{q}}] is an encoder network and [MATH x^{q}] is a query sample (likewise, [MATH k=f_{\textrm{k}}(x^{k})] ). Their instantiations depend on the specific pretext task. The input [MATH x^{q}] and [MATH x^{k}] can be images [27, 59, 61], patches [44], or context consisting a set of patches [44]. The networks [MATH f_{\textrm{q}}] and [MATH f_{\textrm{k}}] can be identical [27, 57, 61], partially shared [44, 34, 2], or different [54].
3.2 Momentum Contrast

From the above perspective, contrastive learning is a way of building a discrete dictionary on high-dimensional continuous inputs such as images. The dictionary is dynamic in the sense that the keys are randomly sampled, and that the key encoder evolves during training. Our hypothesis is that good features can be learned by a large dictionary that covers a rich set of negative samples, while the encoder for the dictionary keys is kept as consistent as possible despite its evolution. Based on this motivation, we present Momentum Contrast as described next.

At the core of our approach is maintaining the dictionary as a queue of data samples. This allows us to reuse the encoded keys from the immediate preceding mini-batches. The introduction of a queue decouples the dictionary size from the mini-batch size. Our dictionary size can be much larger than a typical mini-batch size, and can be flexibly and independently set as a hyper-parameter.

The samples in the dictionary are progressively replaced. The current mini-batch is enqueued to the dictionary, and the oldest mini-batch in the queue is removed. The dictionary always represents a sampled subset of all data, while the extra computation of maintaining this dictionary is manageable. Moreover, removing the oldest mini-batch can be beneficial, because its encoded keys are the most outdated and thus the least consistent with the newest ones.

Using a queue can make the dictionary large, but it also makes it intractable to update the key encoder by back-propagation (the gradient should propagate to all samples in the queue). A naïve solution is to copy the key encoder [MATH f_{\textrm{k}}] from the query encoder [MATH f_{\textrm{q}}] , ignoring this gradient. But this solution yields poor results in experiments (Sec. 4.1). We hypothesize that such failure is caused by the rapidly changing encoder that reduces the key representations’ consistency. We propose a momentum update to address this issue.
Formally, denoting the parameters of [MATH f_{\textrm{k}}] as [MATH \theta_{\textrm{k}}] and those of [MATH f_{\textrm{q}}] as [MATH \theta_{\textrm{q}}] , we update [MATH \theta_{\textrm{k}}] by:
[MATH \small\theta_{\textrm{k}}\leftarrow m\theta_{\textrm{k}}+(1-m)\theta_{\textrm{q}}.] (2)

Here [MATH m\in[0,1)] is a momentum coefficient. Only the parameters [MATH \theta_{\textrm{q}}] are updated by back-propagation. The momentum update in Eqn.(2) makes [MATH \theta_{\textrm{k}}] evolve more smoothly than [MATH \theta_{\textrm{q}}] . As a result, though the keys in the queue are encoded by different encoders (in different mini-batches), the difference among these encoders can be made small. In experiments, a relatively large momentum (e.g., [MATH m] [MATH =] 0.999, our default) works much better than a smaller value (e.g., [MATH m] [MATH =] [MATH 0.9] ), suggesting that a slowly evolving key encoder is a core to making use of a queue.
MoCo is a general mechanism for using contrastive losses. We compare it with two existing general mechanisms in Figure 2. They exhibit different properties on the dictionary size and consistency.

The end-to-end update by back-propagation is a natural mechanism (e.g., [27, 44, 34, 61, 2, 33], Figure 2a). It uses samples in the current mini-batch as the dictionary, so the keys are consistently encoded (by the same set of encoder parameters). But the dictionary size is coupled with the mini-batch size, limited by the GPU memory size. It is also challenged by large mini-batch optimization [23]. Some recent methods [44, 34, 2] are based on pretext tasks driven by local positions, where the dictionary size can be made larger by multiple positions. But these pretext tasks may require special network designs such as patchifying the input [44] or customizing the receptive field size [2], which may complicate the transfer of these networks to downstream tasks.

Another mechanism is the memory bank approach proposed by [59] (Figure 2b). A memory bank consists of the representations of all samples in the dataset. The dictionary for each mini-batch is randomly sampled from the memory bank with no back-propagation, so it can support a large dictionary size. However, the representation of a sample in the memory bank was updated when it was last seen, so the sampled keys are essentially about the encoders at multiple different steps all over the past epoch and thus are less consistent. A momentum update is adopted on the memory bank in [59]. Its momentum update is on the representations of the same sample, not the encoder. This momentum update is irrelevant to our method, because MoCo does not keep track of every sample. Moreover, our method is more memory-efficient and can be trained on billion-scale data, which can be intractable for a memory bank.
Sec. 4 empirically compares these three mechanisms.
bmm: batch matrix multiplication; mm: matrix multiplication; cat: concatenation.
